item.title: Women should not wait for symptoms before cervical cancer screening – Dr Sikiti
item.description: Cervical cancer is one of the most preventable cancers, but women should not wait for symptoms before getting screened. Fiji’s first in-country trained gynaecological oncologist, Dr Nanise Sikiti, says screening is intended for women who feel healthy, as it can detect pre-cancerous changes before they develop into cancer.
item.content:encoded:
Cervical cancer is one of the most preventable cancers, but women should not wait for symptoms before getting screened.

Fiji’s first in-country trained gynaecological oncologist, Dr Nanise Sikiti, says screening is intended for women who feel healthy, as it can detect pre-cancerous changes before they develop into cancer.

Speaking during fijivillage Her-Story with Temalesi Vono, Dr Sikiti says one of the biggest misconceptions about cervical cancer is that it is inevitable and nothing can be done to prevent it.

She says cervical cancer is mainly caused by persistent infection with high-risk types of human papillomavirus, or HPV.

Dr Sikiti says HPV is extremely common, with an estimated 80 percent chance of exposure during a women’s lifetime.

She says HPV should not be associated with shame or judgement, as it is a common virus and the high-risk types that cause most cervical cancers are mainly sexually transmitted.

Insert: Dr Sikiti - Screening is for you Sept 11

Dr Sikiti says there are five gynaecological cancers women should be aware of, including cervical, uterine, ovarian, vaginal and bowel cancers.

She says uterine cancer can present through abnormal bleeding, particularly bleeding after menopause, while ovarian cancer can be more difficult to detect because there is no effective population-based screening test and its symptoms can be vague.

Dr Sikiti says women should know their bodies and pay attention to persistent changes that are different from what is normal for them.

She says warning signs that should not be ignored include persistent bleeding, bleeding between periods, bleeding after intercourse or menopause, abnormal or foul-smelling vaginal discharge, unusual abdominal pain, abdominal swelling and persistent bloating.

However, Dr Sikiti stresses that experiencing these symptoms does not necessarily mean a woman has cancer.

She says they indicate that a woman should be evaluated, as several non-cancerous conditions can cause similar symptoms.

Dr Sikiti says the key message is for women to seek medical attention when they notice that their bodies are not the same as before .

item.description: Also discharged were three-month-old Marina Warren and 11-month-old Jessie Nielsen, both from the Solomon Islands. For Lewenisiga, her daughter’s discharge marks the end of an emotional period that began, when the family discovered that Seruvatu had a heart problem during an outreach programme at Sigatoka Methodist Primary School in March.
item.content:encoded:
Also discharged were three-month-old Marina Warren and 11-month-old Jessie Nielsen, both from the Solomon Islands.

For Lewenisiga, her daughter’s discharge marks the end of an emotional period that began, when the family discovered that Seruvatu had a heart problem during an outreach programme at Sigatoka Methodist Primary School in March.

The diagnosis came as a shock because Seruvatu had been an active child who enjoyed playing rugby and netball.

Lewenisiga says her daughter’s health gradually declined in the months that followed, and after two medical reviews, the family was told that her condition was getting worse and she needed surgery.

The family travelled from Sigatoka to Suva early Saturday morning for the operation, with Lewenisiga spending much of the journey praying and asking God to give her daughter another chance at life.

She says the night before the operation was particularly difficult, and she could not sleep as she waited for her daughter to go into theatre the following morning.

Seruvatu was also afraid, holding onto her mother’s hands before undergoing the operation.

Lewenisiga says watching her daughter go through the experience was not easy , but she remained hopeful and placed her trust in God and the medical team.

She is thankful to the doctors, nurses and staff at the Sri Sathya Sai Sanjeevani Children’s Hospital, as well as the visiting medical team from Singapore, for caring for her daughter.

Lewenisiga says Seruvatu has now been given another chance at life.

She is encouraging other parents to make use of outreach programmes when they are available in their communities and to seek medical assistance if their children need treatment.

item.title: Ledua fails to appear in Suva High Court
item.description: The man accused of attempting to break into the RFMF ammunition magazine building in Nabua in April this year did not appear at the Suva High Court when his case was called yesterday. Isaia Ledua is charged with attempted aggravated burglary.
item.content:encoded:
The man accused of attempting to break into the RFMF ammunition magazine building in Nabua in April this year did not appear at the Suva High Court when his case was called yesterday.

Isaia Ledua is charged with attempted aggravated burglary.

It is alleged that between 8th and 9th April, Ledua attempted to break into the RFMF ammunition magazine building in Nabua and, during the same period, allegedly damaged the door lock keypad.

Defence counsel informed the court that Ledua had been arrested the night before and was in custody at the Nabua Police Station.

The matter has been adjourned to next Thursday.
